catalog_quote: Lepcha morphemes are monosyllabic. Many Lepcha words are composed of different syllables, with the stress usually on the second syllable. Richard Keith Sprigg analyses Lepcha as having contrastive stress (1966b: 199-200). The intonation of Lepcha is characterised by the clustering of syllables into groups, often these are phrases or groups of words marked by suffixes, postpositions or particles. [Plaisier 2006: 24] ... In the pronunciation of dissyllables, whether the word be simple or compound, the accent, as a rule, falls on the last syllable; thus, sa-ryóm, an otter; num-vóm, united in the wedlock, married; ka-jak, the fore-finger; tan to, to know by experience, lá-chók, a whip, to-dat, equality, uniformity, mú-tik, a pearl, &c. [Mainwaring 1876: 138] ... The number of disyllabic nouns in Lepcha is considerable. An overwhelming majority of these have been observed to have low pitch initially, the second syllable being high and either level or falling. A small minority (forty-five) on the other hand, have always been observed to have high pitch initially ... while fifty-two have been observed to have both types of pattern. [Sprigg 1966: 196] ... For Lepcha, therefore, a stress classification is preferred to a tonal classification; and the pivotal forty-six nouns would require a double stress classification (stress 1/2). [Sprigg 1966: 200]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Morphemes are monosyllabic and most words are disyllabic compounds; stress normally falls on the second syllable of the word (= the final syllable of a disyllable; Mainwaring 1876:138 states the same as 'the accent, as a rule, falls on the last syllable' of dissyllables). Sprigg 1966 analyses this as a two-term contrastive stress system: a large majority of nouns (and all verbs) take second-syllable prominence (his 'stress 2', low-high pitch), while a lexically listed minority of nouns take first-syllable prominence ('stress 1', high pitch, greater breath force, long vowel if open), and 46 nouns take either depending on contrastive context. Sprigg explicitly prefers a stress classification over a tonal one for Lepcha.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Sprigg 1966: a minority class of disyllabic nouns (79 in his material, of which 46 alternate with the majority pattern; 13 are Tibetan/Nepali loans, some keeping donor-language pitch) has first-syllable prominence — hence 'contrastive stress' in Plaisier's wording. Mainwaring 1876:138: words compounded with the particle bo and other suffixes carry the accent on the first (substantive) syllable, e.g. mí-bo 'a trance', tóm-bo 'a walker'; in interrogatives the voice rises on the final syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (disyllabic and trisyllabic words). Sprigg notes the choice between the two patterns for the 46 alternating nouns is conditioned by clause-level contrast (contrastive stressing), and Plaisier notes intonation groups syllables into phrases; northern Sikkim intonation differs in tempo. No tone contrast reported (Hyslop 2008:166 'apparently'); Plaisier describes no tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Plaisier's grammar describes the Lepcha of Kalimpong (West Bengal) and Sikkim from fieldwork 1994-98, general language-level lepc1244 (she notes only an intonational difference for northern Sikkim). Sprigg 1966 is based on his own elicited Lepcha material (Kalimpong/Darjeeling area); Mainwaring 1876 describes the Darjeeling and Sikkim hills variety. No dialect-level glottocode applies.

sources.quote: p. 316 (section III.B.1.b 'Unstressed syllables'): "Certain lexical items occur in both a stressed and an unstressed position in disyllabic words, with the result that for them there is a variation in vowel length, between for example, a: in the former position and a in the latter, e.g. -ka: in 'd-kd ' hand ' but ka- in kd-jak ' forefinger' (Mainwaring, 1876, 134, 138). I have the impression that Mainwaring, 1876, uses a in unstressed syllables, e.g. kd-jak, only for stressable lexical items, those which also occur in stressed position, e.g. 'd-kd; otherwise he uses a in unstressed syllables, e.g. sa-'dr, la-vo, fa-li (sa-, la-, fa-; 131, 20, 115); and in this respect his usage is the same as that of the Hooker text: sa-'dr, la-vo, fa-li (-1, 1, 5a). Since the distinction made between ai and in: in stressed syllables (section (a) above) does not apply in unstressed syllables, in which only a occurs, there is sometimes alternation in spelling between a and u" [scanned renders the acute-accented vowel á as 'd']. p. 315 (III.B.1.a 'Stressed syllables'): "In vowel-final syllables, provided that these syllables are stressed, a, a, and e symbolize phonological vowel units characterized…

sources.citation: Mainwaring, G. B. 1876. A Grammar of the Róng (Lepcha) Language as it exists in the Dorjeling and Sikim Hills. Calcutta: Baptist Mission Press.
sources.note: p. 138, '6.—Of Prosody': 'In the pronunciation of dissyllables, whether the word be simple or compound, the accent, as a rule, falls on the last syllable; thus, sa-ryóm, an otter; num-vóm.. married; ka-jak, the fore-finger.. mú-tik, a pearl, &c. In words compounded of the particle bo, and other suffixes, the accent necessarily rests on the first syllable, the substantive part of the word; thus, mí-bo, a trance.. to-mo, trousers, tóm-bo, a walker, &c.' Interrogatives: the voice rises on the final syllable. Verified on the page scan (archive.org public-domain scan).
